text:
# Eventual Consistency

• **Delayed Synchronization**: Data updates are not immediately reflected across all copies in a distributed system; instead, replicas synchronize asynchronously over time, allowing temporary inconsistencies between nodes.

• **High Availability Trade-off**: Systems prioritize availability and partition tolerance over immediate consistency, enabling them to remain responsive even when network failures occur or updates are in progress.

• **Guaranteed Convergence**: All replicas will eventually reach the same state once updates stop propagating, ensuring data consistency is achieved eventually rather than instantaneously.

text:
# Eventual Consistency

• **Delayed Synchronization**: When data is updated in a distributed system, changes don't propagate to all nodes instantly—instead, replicas gradually synchronize over time, meaning different nodes may temporarily have different versions of the same data.

• **Availability Trade-off**: Systems prioritize availability and fault tolerance over immediate consistency, allowing operations to succeed even when some nodes are unreachable, with the guarantee that all nodes will eventually converge to the same state.

• **Use Case Reality**: Commonly found in systems like DNS, social media feeds, and cloud storage, where brief inconsistencies are acceptable in exchange for high performance and resilience to network failures or outages.
